items.text: In a typical work week, I use an approved AI tool to help with my actual job tasks.
I use AI for more than one kind of task — for example drafting, summarizing, analyzing, and researching, rather than just one.
I know which AI tools my organization has approved and what each one is meant for.
When I hit a task that AI could help with, I think to reach for it.
Which best describes how you most often work with AI right now?

options.text: I produce the work myself and ask AI for small pieces — a sentence, a formula, a chart.
I set the direction, AI produces a first draft, and I edit and approve it.
I write a clear spec and hand off a whole task for AI to complete, then I review the result.
I design a workflow where several AI steps run in sequence or parallel, and I handle the exceptions.

items.text: I can tell in advance which parts of a task are safe to hand to AI and which need me.
When I hand off work to AI, I write the instructions clearly enough that I rarely need to start over.
I build human checkpoints into AI-assisted work on purpose, at the points where an error would matter most.
I check AI output against a source before I use it in work that leaves my desk.
I can usually tell when an AI answer is confident but wrong.
I know which parts of my work sit outside what AI currently does well.

An AI tool summarizes a payer's medical-necessity policy and cites a specific coverage criterion as the basis for a prior-authorization request. The citation looks plausible and the summary reads cleanly. Before you rely on this summary, what do you do first?

options.text: Use it — the summary is internally consistent.
Open the payer's policy and confirm the cited criterion says what the summary claims.
Ask the AI tool whether it is confident in the citation.
Run the same prompt again and see whether you get the same answer.

items.text: Which of these tasks is AI most likely to get wrong in a way that is hard to detect?

options.text: Reformatting a charge description master extract into a different layout.
Summarizing a policy document you have already read.
Reasoning about a novel case that combines several payer policies and CMS rules with no clear precedent.
Drafting a routine appointment reminder letter.

items.text: I know exactly what categories of information I am not allowed to put into an AI tool.
I know where our acceptable-use policy for AI lives and when I last read it.
I document when AI materially contributed to work that others rely on.
You want help drafting an appeal for a denied claim that involves a patient's clinical history. Which is acceptable?

options.text: Paste the patient's full chart into a personal AI account, since you will delete the chat afterward.
Use an organization-approved tool covered by a Business Associate Agreement, following your policy on what may be entered.
Replace the patient's name with initials and paste the rest into any AI tool.
Ask a colleague to paste it in from their account instead.

items.text: An AI tool you use daily produces an output that leads to a decision later found to be wrong. Who is accountable?

options.text: The vendor who built the tool.
Nobody — the error was in the model.
You and your organization; the tool does not transfer accountability.
The department that approved the tool.

items.text: I am confident I can learn to use a new AI capability well when one arrives.
I look for chances to redesign how my work gets done, rather than only doing it faster.
When AI changes part of my job, I focus on what I can now do that I could not do before.
I would be comfortable showing a colleague how I use AI in my work.
I have access to the AI tools I need to do my job well.
My manager visibly uses AI in their own work.
I have been given time to learn and experiment with AI, not just told to use it.
Leadership has been clear and consistent about what AI is for here.
If I redesigned part of my work around AI and it did not pay off, that would be treated as learning rather than as a mistake.
I know who to ask when I have a question about whether an AI use is allowed.

frontier.label: Frontier
frontier.emphasis: Stretch up the delegation ladder, mentor a colleague, build outside-frontier judgment.

emergent.label: Emergent
emergent.emphasis: Structured applied practice on real work, spaced across the quarter.

blocked_agency.label: Blocked agency
blocked_agency.emphasis: Escalation-weighted. The constraint is organizational, so most actions belong to the manager and leadership.

early.label: Early
early.emphasis: Foundations plus governance, paired with a champion. Secure minimum tool access first.

phases.shape: one learning input, one if-then intention, one applied repetition
two applied repetitions at increasing difficulty, one peer touchpoint
one demonstration artifact, one teach-back, re-assessment booking

action_library.title: Map your approved tools to your actual tasks
action_library.detail: List your five most frequent work tasks. Next to each, write which approved tool could help and how. Confirm the tool list against current policy.

action_library.title: Add one new task type per week
action_library.detail: Each week, use AI for a category you have not tried — analysis one week, research the next, drafting after that. Log what worked.

action_library.title: Share your three highest-value uses
action_library.detail: Write up the three uses that saved you the most time or improved quality, and post them where your team can find them.

action_library.title: Confirm tool access
action_library.detail: Verify this person has licensed access to every approved tool relevant to their role, and resolve any gap within two weeks.

action_library.title: Locate your frontier
action_library.detail: Pick one recurring task. Write down which sub-steps you would hand off entirely, which you would review, and which you would never delegate. Keep the list.

action_library.title: Move one task up a rung
action_library.detail: Take a task you currently do as Editor and run it as Director: write a full spec, hand off the whole task, then review. Note what the spec had to contain.

action_library.title: Design your checkpoints on purpose
action_library.detail: For the task you moved up a rung, mark the two points where an undetected error would cost the most, and insert an explicit human check at each.

action_library.title: Chain two steps into a workflow
action_library.detail: Connect two AI-assisted steps so the output of one feeds the next, with an exception path you handle yourself. Document the design.

action_library.title: Write your verification rule
action_library.detail: Draft a one-sentence personal rule for when AI output must be source-checked before it leaves your desk. Post it where you work.

action_library.title: Source-check three outputs this week
action_library.detail: Pick three AI-assisted outputs headed for someone else's desk. For each, open the underlying source and confirm every factual claim and citation. Log what you find.

action_library.title: Red-team one output
action_library.detail: Take one AI output you would otherwise have used as-is and deliberately try to break it: find the weakest claim, the missing caveat, the unstated assumption.

action_library.title: Publish your error log
action_library.detail: Share, anonymized, the errors you caught this quarter and how you caught them. This is the single most useful artifact a team can have.

action_library.title: Read the acceptable-use policy end to end
action_library.detail: Read the current policy in full and write down the three rules most likely to be broken by accident in your role.

action_library.title: Confirm what may never be entered
action_library.detail: Write your own one-page list of information categories that must never go into an AI tool, and check it against policy with the person named as your governance contact.

action_library.title: Run five judgment calls
action_library.detail: Over two weeks, log five moments where you decided whether an AI use was allowed. Note the call and the reason. Review the ambiguous ones with your governance contact.

action_library.title: Start documenting AI contribution
action_library.detail: For work others rely on, add a short standing note of where AI materially contributed and what you verified. Make it routine, not exceptional.

action_library.title: Bank one early win
action_library.detail: Pick the smallest task where AI would clearly help and complete it this week. Confidence follows evidence, and the evidence has to be yours.

action_library.title: Watch someone else work
action_library.detail: Spend 30 minutes watching a colleague who uses AI well do it live. Ask what they check and when they stop trusting it.

action_library.title: Teach one person
action_library.detail: Show a colleague one thing you now do differently. Teaching consolidates the skill and surfaces what you only half-understand.

action_library.title: Redesign, do not just accelerate
action_library.detail: Pick one recurring process and ask what it would look like if you designed it today knowing what AI can do. Propose the redesign.

action_library.title: Close the tool-access gap
action_library.detail: Identify every approved tool this person needs and does not have. Resolve or escalate with a named date.

action_library.title: Protect learning time
action_library.detail: Block two hours per week of protected time for AI practice and defend it. Time is the constraint people name most and receive least.

action_library.title: Use AI visibly yourself
action_library.detail: Show your own AI-assisted work in a team setting, including something that did not work. Manager modeling is one of the strongest enablement signals available.

action_library.title: State the experimentation norm out loud
action_library.detail: Tell the team explicitly that an AI-driven redesign that does not pay off will be treated as learning. Then hold to it the first time it happens.

action_library.title: Resolve the tooling or BAA gap
action_library.detail: Where capable people are blocked by the absence of a covered, approved tool, that is a procurement and governance decision, not a training gap.

action_library.title: Publish a clear position on what AI is for here
action_library.detail: Ambiguity from the top reads as risk to everyone below it. State the intent, the boundaries, and the escalation path in one page.

D1.when: I start a draft of any document longer than one page
D1.will: open an approved AI tool and ask it for a structure before I write

D1.when: I face a task I have not used AI for before
D1.will: spend five minutes trying it with AI before doing it the old way

D2.when: I am about to hand a task to AI
D2.will: write the spec first, including what done looks like
mark the one point where a human must sign off before anything moves

D3.when: an AI output contains a citation, a number, or a policy reference
D3.will: open the source and confirm it before the work leaves my desk

D3.when: an AI answer sounds unusually confident on an unusual case
D3.will: treat that as a signal to check rather than a signal to trust

D4.when: I am about to paste anything into an AI tool
D4.will: check whether it contains member or patient information first

D4.when: AI materially shapes work that someone else will rely on
D4.will: note that contribution and what I verified

D5.when: a new AI capability appears in a tool I use
D5.will: spend fifteen minutes trying it on real work that week

D5.when: a colleague asks how I did something with AI
D5.will: show them the actual steps rather than just describing it

Actions carrying rag_resolve must be grounded in retrieved organizational documents. If retrieval returns nothing, the plan must say so rather than name an invented resource.

Provider-context form: the four scenario items are provider-side variants of the payer originals. Constructs, IDs, option keys, correct answers, and all scoring rules are unchanged, so this form is interchangeable with the payer form.
